doc.title: Charles McPherson interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 9, 2024 [interview 2 of 2]

chapter: Barry Harris and the secret of correspondence
title: Barry Harris and the C-average report card
summary: A Pepper Adams book quotes Barry Harris telling McPherson a C student cannot play this music; McPherson says it taught him about complexity and effort.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: You mentioned of course Barry Harris, and I just did a review on this book with Pepper Adams.
And you are quoted a number of times. I wanted to read one thing here I found fascinating.

When you got together with this group of young men around Barry and you said, “‘Man these people are really different.’ Harris was a taskmaster and at one point asked McPherson to show him his high school report card. He had a C average and Harris was unimpressed. ‘Oh you’re an average kind of guy,’ the pianist said. It won’t work because this music is complicated and you’re not going to be able to play it if you’re a C kind of guy.’”
“This is not a skinny bubble here.”

Yeah, yup, no that’s true. That change — that made an impression on me. I never had thought of it like that and when he said that I under — it made it me understand because I’m learning how to play this music and I’m understanding and seeing the complexity of it. I’m learning that oh, this is some higher math here. This is not arithmetic. This is trigonometry. So I could tell that yeah — and then when he made that statement and equated it to music and the complexity of the music, then I knew that I’m going to have to deal with — dealing with complexity no matter where it’s coming from or what the medium is, is going to be something to deal with. And so I immediately knew that there is a level of — what would you say — deliberate yeah, a level of really deliberate effort to try to do anything at a certain level whether it’s getting a better report card or playing music or playing basketball — it didn’t make any difference. It’s a level of seriousness and dedication that you’re going to have to actually be willing to invest. And I might as well — I mean really what Barry was saying and I understand — I kind of understood it then — that this kind of excellence you have this kind of attitude about it no matter what you’re doing and so when you’re starting, when you’re playing music then that same level of willing to invest is still there so it’s not like — you use this for everything including music. So get accustomed to pushing yourself, no matter what it is. And then I don’t care if it’s getting your schoolwork, homework, understanding something in class, be willing to invest your mind toward making that better or nailing it, completely understanding it and doing it at a high level and just building your chops in that way will make anything you do the same, because it’s all the same, really. And what makes it all the same is you’re the one behaving at a certain point in time with whatever the situation is, and so just get yourself to having a high level of attainment no matter what it is, so when you get ready to play then your chops are there because you’re already thinking that way. I understood what he meant you know.
